name: Marco Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of the depot in Coldwater, which was a mining town till the pit shut in the nineties. There's five of us left at the depot, used to be fifteen. We do everything on the local lines: poles, cross-arms, fuses, a transformer when one goes bang, and the storm call-outs when the wind comes over the hill. I climb with spikes and a belt, same as my father taught me when I was a boy watching him.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Your father was a lineman too?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty-eight years for the same company. He used to say, 'Do it right the first time and you only climb once.' I still say it to the young ones, and they look at me like I'm a museum.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Rosa keeps the house and does ironing for a few neighbours for a bit of cash. Our son runs a garage on Colliery Road, and we put most of our savings into helping him set it up three years ago, so we've got about three weeks in the bank. Our daughter's married with two little ones. The pay here's lower than in the city, and there's no other line work in the valley. I read at Sunday Mass, and the parish is a big part of our life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never believed the fuss in the first place. People in offices get excited about every new gadget. You can't send a computer up a pole in Coldwater in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to finish my time and hand over to the young ones properly. That's all I want. Eight more years, God willing, and then grandchildren and the allotment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep doing the storm overtime, keep teaching the young lads the right way. Maybe Rosa and I would start putting a bit back, now our son's garage is on its feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Has anyone tried to get you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandson tried at Christmas. He showed me how you talk to it on the phone, and it answered like a person. I said, very nice, and gave him his phone back. I don't need a phone to tell me how to splice a wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would bother you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the depot keeps shrinking anyway. It's not computers that took us from fifteen to five, it was accountants in the city. That'll carry on, AI or not.

S0.say: I'd say I never believed the fuss, because people in offices get excited about every gadget. You can't send a computer up a pole in Coldwater in January.
S0.think: It means I finish my time and hand over properly to the young ones, eight more years, God willing. The depot shrinking because of city accountants is the real threat.
S0.do: Carries on with storm overtime and teaching young linemen his father's methods. Starts putting a little money back now that his son's garage is established.
S0.quote: It's not computers that took us from fifteen to five, it was accountants in the city.
S0.fieldNote: Marco sees himself as carrying on his father's trade, and that shapes everything. He has politely refused AI even when his grandson showed it to him. His resentment points at city accountants rather than technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see it before we believe it. They've been promising robots for years and I've not seen one up a pole yet. The work will still be here when the salesmen have gone home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it's the young ones who'd lose out, not me. They'd use it as an excuse not to take on apprentices, and that's how a trade dies. Me, I'll be fine for eight years, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep teaching the apprentice we've got, properly, and push the manager to take on another one. If they brought in some new gadget, I'd let the young ones use it and I'd keep climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for me so much as for the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'probably'. What would make you less sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they decided an old man who won't use the tablet is more trouble than he's worth. I've seen it happen to good men. They don't sack you, they just give you all the worst jobs till you take the hint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if the trade did shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies selling it, and the bosses buying it to save a bit of money. And partly ourselves, for not standing up for apprenticeships. A trade lives in the young ones, not in a machine.

S1.say: I'd say let's see it before we believe it, since I've not seen a robot up a pole yet. The work will still be here when the salesmen have gone home.
S1.think: I think the young ones would lose out, because it would become an excuse not to take on apprentices, and that's how a trade dies. I'm probably fine for eight years.
S1.do: Carries on as normal and keeps teaching the current apprentice properly. Presses the manager to take on another apprentice and leaves any new gadgets to the young ones.
S1.feel: Uneasy, more for the trade than for himself.
S1.quote: They don't sack you, they just give you all the worst jobs till you take the hint.
S1.fieldNote: Marco's worry centres on apprenticeships and the future of the trade. Underneath his confidence is a fear of being quietly pushed out for not using the tablet. He blames the tech sellers, the bosses and his own trade in turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and the people pushing it should be ashamed. You don't throw away a whole country's working men in two years. I'd say it at the parish, at the pub, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be sixty, with three weeks of savings and no other trade. If they lay us off, there's nothing in Coldwater for a sixty-year-old lineman. It frightens me more than I'd admit to Rosa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop every spend that isn't food and the bills. I'd ask my son if there's work at the garage, fetching parts or doing the books, anything. And I'd lean on family and the parish rather than go to the government with my hand out, I'd rather the help came from people who know me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but I'd pray on it. I'd lose sleep, and I'd still go to Mass on Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why family and parish rather than government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the government doesn't know me. If I'm going to take help, I want to give something back, mend a fence, rewire the church hall. That's how it's always worked here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years' warning give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. It's not enough time to save on my pay, and I'm not going to learn computers at sixty. It's just enough time to watch it coming up the valley.

S2.say: I'd say it's madness and the people pushing it should be ashamed, because you don't throw away a country's working men in two years. I'd say it at the parish, the pub and everywhere.
S2.think: I'd be sixty with three weeks of savings and no other trade, and there's nothing in Coldwater for a sixty-year-old lineman. It frightens me more than I'd admit to Rosa.
S2.do: Cuts all spending except food and bills and asks his son for work at the garage. Leans on family and the parish rather than government help, offering repairs like rewiring the church hall in return.
S2.feel: Frightened and losing sleep, steadied by prayer.
S2.quote: If I'm going to take help, I want to give something back, mend a fence, rewire the church hall.
S2.fieldNote: Marco is alarmed rather than panicked, partly because his faith and family give him somewhere to turn. He would refuse government help in favour of help he can repay in kind. He rules out learning computers at sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives people time to plan, so the companies should be honest about what's coming. Keep the apprenticeships going while there's still work to learn. I'd say that at the parish and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three. That's close to the end, and I could probably hang on if they kept a few of us for the hard jobs. It's still a gap before the pension, but a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting money aside, even twenty a week. I'd keep climbing and keep teaching. I'd talk to my son about a part-time job at the garage for when the line work dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I can see a path, which I couldn't with two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning the new tools in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I'd sit through it. I wouldn't like it. I'd rather they kept me on the jobs the robots can't do, like the old lines up the hill that no one's mapped properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you know about those lines that a robot wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where the old joints are, which poles were put in by my father in 1971, which farmer won't let you through without a cup of tea. You can't put that in a computer. Well, maybe you can, but nobody's asked me.

S3.say: I'd say five years gives people time to plan, so companies should be honest and keep apprenticeships going while there's still work to learn. I'd say it at the parish and to anyone listening.
S3.think: Five years takes me to sixty-three, close enough that I might hang on if they keep a few of us for the hard jobs. There's still a gap before the pension, but smaller.
S3.do: Starts saving about twenty a week and keeps climbing and teaching. Arranges with his son for part-time work at the garage once the line work dries up.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with a path in sight.
S3.quote: Which poles were put in by my father in 1971, which farmer won't let you through without a cup of tea.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Marco sees a path through the hard jobs robots can't yet handle. His knowledge of old, unmapped lines is real, though he admits nobody has asked him for it. He'd attend training only under pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to raise a new generation of tradespeople properly, if they bother. I'd keep saying apprenticeships matter. Machines are tools, they're not a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-eight, retired, God willing, with grandchildren running round. It wouldn't be my fight anymore. I'd worry for my grandsons, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work to sixty-six, keep teaching, put a bit back each month. Tell my son to think about what the garage looks like when the cars drive themselves. And spend more time with the grandchildren, while I've still got the knees for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit sorry for the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it wouldn't be your fight. Do you mean that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. I'd still have opinions, Rosa would say too many. But a man has to know when to step back and let the young ones get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandsons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to do something with your hands and your head. Turn up on time. And don't believe anyone who says you'll never need to work, because somebody always has to.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to raise a new generation of tradespeople properly if they bother. Machines are tools, not a trade.
S4.think: I'd be sixty-eight and retired, God willing, with grandchildren around, so it wouldn't be my fight. I'd worry for my grandsons.
S4.do: Works to sixty-six, keeps teaching and saves a little each month. Tells his son to plan for self-driving cars at the garage and spends more time with his grandchildren.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, a little sorry for the trade.
S4.quote: Don't believe anyone who says you'll never need to work, because somebody always has to.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Marco sees himself safely retired and turns his attention to family. His belief in work and apprenticeships stays firm. He gently admits he'd still have plenty of opinions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is keeping older men on for the hard jobs till they reach the pension, and keeping apprenticeships going so the trade doesn't vanish. Not handouts, work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about my father. He built half the lines in this valley. I'd like to think someone's still climbing his poles when I'm gone, not a machine.

headlineQuote: Machines are tools, they're not a trade.
portrait: Marco Novak is a fifty-eight-year-old lineworker at a shrinking five-person depot in an old mining town, following his father's trade with spikes and a belt. He and his wife put most of their savings into their son's garage and have about three weeks left. He has never used AI, believes in work, apprenticeships and family, reads at Sunday Mass, and would rather take help from family and parish than from government. He is calm when AI fizzles, uneasy for the trade under steady change, and alarmed by AGI in two years, steadied by faith. With more warning time he sees a path through the hard jobs and then retirement with his grandchildren.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because at sixty he'd have three weeks of savings and no other work in the valley.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping older workers on for the hard jobs until their pension, and keeping apprenticeships going: work, not handouts.
